name: Tomas Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two injection moulding presses at a plastics plant that makes car interior parts, mostly air vent surrounds and glovebox hinges. The press does the moulding, my job is to pull the parts, trim the flash, that's the thin extra plastic around the edges, and check them against the sample board. I'm on rotating shifts, so this week it's two in the afternoon to ten at night. I still miss short shots sometimes, where the mould doesn't fill all the way, and the quality lady, Agnes, catches them and gives me a look.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and the worst part of it for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is the pay, honestly, it's better than most places around here because of the night shifts, and Ines and I are saving for a flat. Worst part is the heat off the presses in summer and the feeling that I'm a pair of hands the machine hasn't quite replaced yet. There's already a robot arm on the big press at the end that does the pulling, and the guy who used to work it now just watches it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now can we talk about the stuff that actually matters, like pay and shift patterns. I'd probably share some article about it being a bubble with a sarcastic comment. Ines would roll her eyes at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It wouldn't change much for me. The robot arms were coming anyway, AI or no AI, so the real question is still how many presses one person looks after. I'd still want to move up to setting the moulds, because the setters are the ones they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving for the flat, about seven hundred a month, and ask my supervisor about the mould setter training that comes up every spring. I'd keep using the AI chat thing now and then, like when I asked it to explain what a hot runner was. Nothing else really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like the news promised a storm and it rained for ten minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the guy who now watches the robot arm. What do you think about when you see him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think, that's me in five years if I'm not careful. His name is Pieter, he's nice, but he looks bored out of his mind. He told me the arm is better than him at pulling parts and he doesn't even mind, he just wishes they'd let him do something with his brain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mould setter, specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because setting a mould is fiddly, you're bolting in a two-tonne tool, connecting the water lines, getting the temperatures right. The robots can't do it yet, and the setters earn more. It's the next step up, and the training is paid.

S0.say: I'd say good, now let's talk about what matters, like pay and shift patterns. I'd share an article calling it a bubble with a sarcastic comment.
S0.think: Privately he thinks little changes because robot arms were coming anyway; the real question is how many presses one person runs. He still wants to become a mould setter because setters are the ones kept.
S0.do: Keeps saving about seven hundred a month for a flat with Ines and asks about the spring mould setter training. Keeps using an AI chat tool now and then to explain technical terms.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a promised storm that turned into ten minutes of rain.
S0.quote: He told me the arm is better than him at pulling parts and he doesn't even mind, he just wishes they'd let him do something with his brain.
S0.fieldNote: He separates AI from robot arms and sees the robots as the real story at his plant. Pieter, the operator turned watcher, is his warning picture. He's already planning a step up to mould setter regardless of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules. If a plant automates and makes more money, part of that should go to retraining the people it moved, and the union should have a say in how fast it goes. I'd say that at the canteen and I'd say it at the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be fine, actually, but only if I move up. The trimming and checking I do now is exactly the kind of thing a camera and a robot arm can take. I'd want to see the first few plants do it before I believed it, but once I saw it, I'd move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the mould setter course the first spring it's offered, and maybe a night class on basic robot maintenance if the plant pays for it. I'd ask a mate at the plant across town how they're handling it. We'd keep saving for the flat, maybe buy a bit smaller than we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not panic, it's more like a pebble in my shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a smaller flat. What changes in the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were looking at two bedrooms near Ines's school. If my job's wobbly, we'd go one bedroom and a smaller mortgage, so we could cover it on her pay alone if we had to. Teachers aren't paid much, but they're paid steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see other plants do it first. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the big supplier on the industrial estate, the one that does door panels, put in camera inspection and actually cut operators. Then I'd know it works and it's not a sales pitch. I don't jump on the first thing, but I don't stand still once it's proven.

S1.say: I'd say this is where we need rules: plants that automate and profit should fund retraining, and unions should have a say in the pace. I'd say it in the canteen and at the union meeting.
S1.think: He thinks he'd be fine only if he moves up, because his trimming and checking is exactly what a camera and robot arm can take. He'd wait to see other plants do it, then move.
S1.do: Signs up for mould setter training the first spring it's offered and takes a robot maintenance night class if the plant pays. Asks a friend at another plant how they cope and plans a smaller flat with Ines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a pebble in his shoe rather than panic.
S1.quote: Teachers aren't paid much, but they're paid steady.
S1.fieldNote: His steady style shows clearly: he waits for proof from the door panel plant, then commits. Housing plans adjust before job plans do. His public line is about rules and union say; privately he's thinking about his own next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a failure of government, plain and simple. They saw it coming and they let a few companies race each other without any brakes. I'd be out protesting and I'd be telling everyone to join a union while it still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years and the presses run themselves, the setters too probably. Ines's job is in trouble as well, if AI can teach. We'd go from saving for a flat to wondering what we live on, and our savings are good, but they're not two-lifetimes good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop the flat search straight away and keep renting, and I'd keep the deposit money in the bank. I'd join every bit of union action and whatever political campaign was pushing for a basic income. I'd ask the plant for any job going on the robot side, even cleaning them, to stay inside as long as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd been doing everything right and it didn't matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd done everything right. What would you say to Ines that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's not buy anything for a year and just see. She'd probably say the kids in her class still need a person, and I'd want to believe her. Then we'd sit there with the flat listings still open on the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wait for proof before moving. In two years, there's no time for proof. What then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exactly the problem. My whole way of doing things is to watch someone else go first, and here there's no first, everyone goes at once. So I'd fall back on the union, because that's the one thing you can join without needing proof.

S2.say: I'd say this is a plain failure of government, letting a few companies race with no brakes. I'd be out protesting and telling everyone to join a union while it still means something.
S2.think: In two years the presses and maybe the setters are automated, and Ines's teaching job is at risk too. Their savings are good but not enough to replace two incomes for long.
S2.do: Stops the flat search and keeps the deposit in the bank. Joins union action and campaigns for a basic income, and asks for any role on the robot side, even cleaning, to stay employed as long as possible.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with the bitter sense that doing everything right didn't matter.
S2.quote: Then we'd sit there with the flat listings still open on the laptop.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario removes his favourite move, waiting for proof, and he says so himself. Two exposed incomes make this personal rather than abstract. He falls back on collective action because it needs no proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a government to get a plan in place, so get on with it. Robot tax, public retraining, a guaranteed income at the end. I'd say it at the union and I'd vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to watch it happen to someone else first, which is how I like to do things. I'd see which plants automate in year one and two and what happens to their people. By year three I'd know where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the mould setter course in the first year anyway, because it's paid and it keeps me useful for longer. In year two or three I'd start looking at jobs that need a person in the room, maybe something in public services, using the AI chat tools more to help me study. We'd hold off buying the flat until we know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. Like a long exam where you can see the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of public service job do you picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know yet. Ines says I'd be good with teenagers, I coach a youth football team on Saturdays. Maybe something like a youth worker, but I'd want to see if those jobs still exist in year three before I bet on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at your plant would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnes in quality, she's fifty-something and she's been checking parts for thirty years. Cameras will do her job before mine. She doesn't have the years left to start again and she doesn't have the years left to retire either.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for a government plan, so get on with it: a robot tax, public retraining and a guaranteed income at the end. I'd say it at the union and vote on it.
S3.think: Five years suits his style because he can watch others go first. He'd see which plants automate in years one and two and know his direction by year three.
S3.do: Does the paid mould setter course in year one to stay useful longer. In years two or three looks at jobs that need a person in the room, like youth work, using AI chat tools to study, and holds off on the flat.
S3.feel: Anxious but in control, like a long exam with the clock in view.
S3.quote: She doesn't have the years left to start again and she doesn't have the years left to retire either.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him back his preferred rhythm of watching then moving. His Saturday football coaching hints at a direction he hasn't fully claimed. His worry for older colleagues like Agnes is sharper than his worry for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Shorter working weeks, retraining paid for by the companies that profit, and a proper safety net at the end. If we waste ten years, that's on the politicians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough time to change careers properly, maybe twice. I think I'd actually be okay in this one, as long as the end isn't everyone sitting at home with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the smaller flat in the first couple of years, because then at least the roof is ours before anything hits. I'd do the setter course, then in year three or four start proper training for youth work or something like it. I'd stay in the union and push for a shorter week deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than the others. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd hold off on the flat, now you'd buy it. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two or five years, I don't want a mortgage I can't pay. With ten, I'd want the flat paid down as much as possible before it hits. A roof you own is the only thing a robot can't take off you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said as long as the end isn't everyone sitting at home. What does that worry look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture my dad after his factory closed when I was twelve. He got a payout, he was fine for money, but he sat in front of the TV for two years. That's the bit that scares me, more than the money.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it: shorter weeks, company-funded retraining and a proper safety net. If we waste it, that's on the politicians.
S4.think: At thirty-seven when it lands, he'd have time to change careers properly, maybe twice. He thinks he'd be okay, provided the end doesn't leave everyone idle at home.
S4.do: Buys the smaller flat early to pay down the roof before change hits. Does the setter course, then starts youth work training around year three or four, and stays in the union pushing for a shorter week.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, with room to breathe.
S4.quote: A roof you own is the only thing a robot can't take off you.
S4.fieldNote: His housing decision flips with the timeline, which shows careful thinking about debt. The deepest fear surfaces late: his father's idleness after a factory closure, not money. Ten years lets his steady style work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I do relies on watching others go first, and that one gives nobody time to go first. What would help is the government guaranteeing an income straight away, and a real job guarantee, so people like my dad aren't left on the sofa.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my dad, and I think he explains a lot of how I answered. When his factory shut, everyone talked about the money, nobody talked about what he'd do on a Tuesday. If AGI comes, somebody needs to think about the Tuesdays.

headlineQuote: If AGI comes, somebody needs to think about the Tuesdays.
portrait: Tomas Olsen is a 27-year-old junior injection moulding operator at a plastics plant making car interior parts, saving with his partner Ines, a primary school teacher, for a flat. He's progressive and a union member, uses AI tools now and then, and changes course once he's seen something work elsewhere. He's calm if AI stalls and uneasy in steady change, aiming for a mould setter role. A two-year AGI alarms him because there's no time to watch others go first, while five and ten years give back his rhythm. Behind it all is his father, who sat idle for two years after his factory closed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it gives nobody time to go first and he relies on watching others before he moves.
whatWouldHelp: An immediate guaranteed income plus a real job guarantee, so people aren't left with nothing to do.
